name: Andrei Shleifer

summary.text: Andrei Shleifer is a Harvard economics professor who directed the Harvard Institute for International Development's USAID-funded advisory project in Russia, where he was assigned to work with Anatoly Chubais on privatization. HIID removed him from the Russia programs in 1997 after USAID alleged conflicts of interest. In the U.S. government's civil suit, a federal judge found in June 2004 that he was liable on one of five counts (conspiracy to help Jonathan Hay commit fraud) and a jury found in December 2004 that he had been assigned to Russia; the case settled in 2005 with Shleifer paying $2 million and accepting a two-year USAID debarment, without admitting liability.

facts.claim: Shleifer was assigned to work with Anatoly Chubais on privatization in the Harvard advisory project in Russia, while Jeffrey Sachs advised Yegor Gaidar on macroeconomics.
facts.quote: Shleifer was assigned to work with Chubais on privatization, while Sachs advised Gaidar on macroeconomics.

facts.claim: According to Institutional Investor, in July 1994 Shleifer and his wife Nancy Zimmerman began investing in Russia, which the magazine described as a direct violation of his contract and of the restrictions imposed by USAID and Harvard. The 2004 court opinion records that in the summer of 1994 Shleifer invited Hay to invest in Russian oil stocks with him.
facts.quote: in the summer of 1994, Shleifer invited Hay to invest in Russian oil stocks with him.

facts.claim: In 1997 USAID alleged that Shleifer's wife had made investments in Russia using Harvard resources and staff paid by the U.S. government; Shleifer denied wrongdoing through his lawyer, and HIID dismissed him from its Russia programs.
facts.quote: The agency alleged that Jonathan Hay had invested in Russian government bonds in violation of its conflict-of-interest rules, and that Andrei Shleifer's wife, Nancy Zimmerman, had made similar investments using Harvard resources and staff paid by the U.S. government. Through their lawyers, both Shleifer and Hay denied wrongdoing. HIID dismissed Hay and Shleifer from their work on the Russia programs.

Harvard in Russia: Conflicts of Interest (repost of the July-August 1997 article)

facts.claim: On June 28, 2004, Judge Douglas P. Woodlock found Shleifer liable on one of five charges, conspiracy to help Hay commit fraud, and held that Shleifer and Hay were making individual investments for individual benefit rather than acting within the scope of their Harvard employment. The judge rejected the argument that Shleifer was merely a consultant exempt from the conflict rules but said he lacked enough evidence to decide whether Shleifer had been assigned to Russia.
facts.quote: the judge did find Shleifer liable on one of five charges: that of conspiracy to help Hay commit fraud. [...] Woodlock asserted that he did not have enough evidence to determine whether Shleifer was actually assigned to the project country (i.e., Russia), one of the requirements needed to define a conflict of interest.

facts.claim: In December 2004 a federal jury in Boston concluded that Shleifer had been assigned to Russia, resolving the remaining fraud count against him.
facts.quote: The 12 jurors, many of whom appeared to snooze through some of the trial's most technical testimony, took just four hours to conclude that, indeed, Shleifer had been assigned to Russia.

sources.title: Feds Win Dispute In HIID Lawsuit

facts.claim: Under the August 2005 settlement Shleifer agreed to pay $2 million to the government and was debarred from USAID work for two years; a firm owned by his wife had already paid the government $1.5 million. He did not admit liability and remained a tenured Harvard professor (the Jones professor of economics).
facts.quote: Shleifer agreed to pay $2 million to the government [...] A firm owned by Shleifer's wife had already paid the government $1.5 million. [...] Shleifer has also been disbarred from USAID work for two years

connections.claim: Shleifer directed HIID's USAID-funded Russia Project; the court described him and Hay as senior supervisory figures at the project. HIID removed him from the Russia programs in 1997.
connections.quote: Shleifer and Hay, who were senior supervisory figures at the Russia Project, nevertheless wrongfully invested and conducted business in Russia, resulting in a breach of the contract by Harvard.
